rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5 (line 272): containment, monotone expected maximum, and the null-win statement
rows.evidence: unchanged since d10fb51 (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived. Let Q_N be the maximum of N null statistics and X_N the new null. Q_N = max(Q_(N-1), X_N) >= Q_(N-1) pointwise, for any joint law of the statistics. (a) E[Q_N] >= E[Q_(N-1)]: the expected maximum cannot fall as N grows. (b) {Z + delta > Q_N} is a subset of {Z + delta > Q_(N-1)}, so the probability that the genuine configuration wins cannot rise (containment, the T span that was already at 584f614). (c) The complement: P(some null beats the genuine) = 1 - P(genuine wins) cannot fall, so 'the null configurations win at least as often' (T). Bound: Lesson 1 Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82) states 'Let Z_1, ..., Z_N each have the standard normal distribution, with any joint distribution, and N >= 2. Then E[max Z_n] <= sqrt(2 ln N)'; its proof (Jensen, e^(lambda E M) <= sum E e^(lambda Z_n) = N e^(lambda^2/2), then lambda = sqrt(2 ln N)) is re-derived and holds with no independence. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l08_sec5_monotone.py, seed 777, 60,000 draws, N up to 60; output out_l08_sec5_monotone.txt): E[max] of the first N is non-decreasing in N for an equicorrelated law (rho 0.9), independent normals, a comonotone law and a block-random law; at every N it lies below sqrt(2 ln N) (smallest margins 0.9973, 0.5416, 1.1820 and 0.5990); P(genuine wins) with k nulls, k = 1..39, is non-increasing (0.8778, 0.8185, 0.7111, 0.6612, 0.5417, ... ). All checks pass.

rows.evidence: unchanged since d10fb51 (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-checked. The back now says only what Proposition 5.4 proves: "It uses V1 + V2 instead of theta. For jointly normal returns with a common per-period Sharpe ratio SR and SR^2 < 2 (Proposition 5.4) it is undersized under positive correlation and oversized under negative correlation. In general it is oversized exactly when theta > V1 + V2." Proposition 5.4 (line 426-428) gives the limit 2(1 - Phi(z sqrt((V1+V2)/theta))), which is below alpha when theta < V1+V2 and above when theta > V1+V2. Re-derived: Corollary 5.2 gives theta = 2(1-rho) + (SR1^2 + SR2^2)/2 - SR1 SR2 rho^2 and V_i = 1 + SR_i^2/2, so for a common SR, theta - (V1+V2) = -rho(2 + SR^2 rho), whose sign is -sign(rho) when SR^2 < 2 (since 2 + SR^2 rho >= 2 - SR^2 > 0). Monte Carlo (4e6 draws, scratch math_checks.py, math_checks_out.txt) confirms the closed form for theta to 0.0035 at the largest deviation across rho in {-0.9,...,0.9} and three SR pairs. No numbers on this card. T is correct. [8352c53: cards.json changed for S7-c154, S7-c161 and S7-c219 and gained S7-c223 (L07) and other units' cards; this card is unchanged (git diff checked).]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c212 (L08, new, grade T); course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5; key-results row 858
rows.evidence: unchanged since d10fb51 (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Claim: adding a null trial cannot raise the probability that a genuine configuration wins in sample, whatever the joint law. Proof (re-derived): let X0 be the genuine in-sample statistic and M_k the maximum of k null statistics. The winning event with k nulls is {X0 > M_k}; adding a null Y gives {X0 > max(M_k, Y)}, which is contained in {X0 > M_k}, so its probability cannot exceed the earlier one. No independence or distributional assumption is used. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/spot_checks.py, 400,000 draws, a common-factor joint law, N-1 = 0,1,4,9,39 nulls): the win probability is non-increasing at every size (for example 0.6448 -> 0.4817 when a second null is added, 0.0513 -> 0.0502 at 39 nulls). The card's back matches Section 5's text. Grade T is right (a proof on the page). PASS. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Corollary 5.2 (line 405-410), Proposition 5.4 (line 425-431), key-results rows 747-748
rows.evidence: unchanged since d10fb51 (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: New row; re-derived and spot-checked numerically (scratch math_checks.py, output math_checks_out.txt). Influence of the Sharpe estimator for standardized return u: psi = u - (SR/2)(u^2 - 1); Var psi = 1 + SR^2/2; Cov(psi1, psi2) = rho + SR1 SR2 rho^2 / 2 (Isserlis: E[u1 u2] = rho, E[u1 u2^2] = 0, E[u1^2 u2^2] = 1 + 2 rho^2). Hence theta = Var(psi1 - psi2) = 2(1 - rho) + (SR1^2 + SR2^2)/2 - SR1 SR2 rho^2, the Corollary 5.2 formula (row 747). Monte Carlo with 4,000,000 draws for SR pairs (0.05,0.05), (0.1,0.3), (0.5,1.0) and rho in {-0.9,-0.5,0,0.5,0.9}: largest |MC - closed form| = 0.0035, consistent with MC error. Sign check (common SR in {0.05, 0.5, 1.3, 1.41}, rho in +-{0.1, 0.5, 0.99}): sign(theta - (V1+V2)) = -sign(rho) for every point. So Proposition 5.4's "undersized under positive correlation, oversized under negative" holds for SR^2 < 2. The limit (line 427) follows from Theorem 5.1, sqrt((T-1)/T) -> 1 and Slutsky's lemma, as the proof on lines 433-436 states; the proof's identity (V1+V2) - theta = rho(2 + SR^2 rho) (line 436) matches the derivation above. PASS. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5, T span (line 272): 'The luck, the expected maximum of the nulls, cannot fall as N grows, because adding a null can only raise the maximum; for standard normal null statistics with any joint law it is at most sqrt(2 ln N) (Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since d10fb51 (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. Monotonicity: with N+1 nulls the maximum is the pointwise maximum over N nulls and one more variable, so it is at least the N-null maximum for every outcome, and its expectation cannot fall. Bound: for any joint law of Z_1..Z_N standard normal, e^{lambda E max Z_n} <= E e^{lambda max Z_n} (Jensen) <= sum_n E e^{lambda Z_n} = N e^{lambda^2/2}, so E max Z_n <= ln N / lambda + lambda/2 for every lambda > 0; lambda = sqrt(2 ln N) gives sqrt(2 ln N). The statement matches Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82), whose scope is 'any joint distribution', and the L08 claim uses no wider scope. The index is the page's N (configurations), and the claim uses the N-1 nulls, with sqrt(2 ln(N-1)) <= sqrt(2 ln N). Concept link to L01 def-expected-maximum-sharpe exists (check_dag PASS). Card S7-c227 now covers it (L08-sec5-expected-max-card-gap).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c066 (L07, grade T)
rows.evidence: Front: at a positive SR, what does negative skewness do to the standard error and through which term? Back: 'It enlarges it, through -gamma3 SR, which is positive when gamma3 < 0 < SR, holding the kurtosis term fixed. The normal formula flatters negatively skewed strategies when the kurtosis is at least 3, because then (gamma4 - 3)SR^2/4 >= 0 as well.' Checked: V = 1 - gamma3 SR + (gamma4-1)/4 SR^2 (formula (1)); holding gamma4 fixed, dV/dgamma3 = -SR < 0, so negative skewness enlarges V through -gamma3 SR; V - V_normal = -gamma3 SR + (gamma4-3)SR^2/4 (exact rational check, 0 failures). The second sentence is the second half of the Shape T span in section 7 (line 539), with the kurtosis condition the round-15 verifier required (the round-15 counterexample gamma3 = -0.5, gamma4 = 1.25, SR = 3 has V - V_normal = -2.4375). One T statement, so the card is atomic. T grade is right (proved on page).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204): T span 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite, sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) -> N(0,1), by the CLT for mu-hat, the LLN for sigma-hat and Slutsky's lemma'
rows.evidence: Derivation re-checked step by step. (i) SR-hat = mu-hat/sigma-hat, so sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) is an identity. (ii) With iid returns, mean mu = SR sigma = 0 and finite variance sigma^2, the CLT gives sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma -> N(0,1). (iii) sigma-hat^2 = (1/(T-1)) sum (r - r-bar)^2 -> sigma^2 in probability by the LLN applied to r^2 (finite since E r^2 < infinity) and r-bar -> 0; so sigma/sigma-hat -> 1 in probability (the divisor T or T-1 does not matter). (iv) Slutsky gives the limit N(0,1). Nothing beyond finite variance is used. Numerical spot check (scratch num_checks.py, 20000 replications): Student t with 3 df scaled to unit variance, SR = 0: P(z <= -1.6449) = 0.0513 / 0.0502 / 0.0502 and P(z <= 1.6449) = 0.9505 / 0.9500 / 0.9506 at T = 250 / 1000 / 4000 (N(0,1): 0.05 and 0.95); sd(z) = 1.007 / 1.001 / 0.992. The fourth moment is infinite there, so the check is of the claim's sufficiency. Grade T is right (proved on the page). The iid standing assumption is the section 1 assumption ('keep independence').

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204) and section 7 bullet (line 539): B span, data-cite gine1997student, data-locator Abstract: 'Giné, Götze and Mason show ... the Student t-statistic is asymptotically standard normal if and only if the observations lie in the domain of attraction of the normal law'

The span says the same, with 'observations' for the iid sample. Scope: iid observations (the section 1 standing assumption). The zero-SR scope is supplied by 'At a zero Sharpe ratio' (mean zero). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html section 7, bullet 'Shape' (line 539): T span 'For a positive Sharpe ratio and kurtosis at least 3 ... (Example 1.4 is such a case)'
rows.evidence: Algebra: V = 1 - g3 SR + (g4-1)/4 SR^2 (formula (1)); V - (1 + SR^2/2) = -g3 SR + ((g4-1)/4 - 1/2) SR^2 = -g3 SR + (g4-3)/4 SR^2. Exact rational identity at 20000 random points: 0 failures (scratch num_checks.out). Sign: with SR > 0, g3 < 0 the first term is strictly positive; with g4 >= 3 the second is nonnegative; so V > 1 + SR^2/2 (20000 random points with the three conditions: 0 violations). Example 1.4 (line 88-92): SR = 0.1 > 0, g3 = -2 < 0, g4 = 9 >= 3, and V = 1.22 > 1.005 (checked). 'Understates the variance' is the same statement as V > V_normal. 'Flatters negatively skewed strategies' is the interpretation (the SR looks more precise than it is). Grade T is right (proved on the page).
